Research has found that larger transformer models produce surpival estimates that do not align with human reading patterns as the model size increases. This study investigates why this discrepancy occurs by comparing the surpival predictions of BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet models across varying sizes. The results reveal that while these models share similar surpival performance, the models exhibit distinct prediction patterns with a notable difference in how they weight token probabilities. The analysis also shows that larger models struggle to capture time-related information in sentences. Ultimately, this study suggests that accurately modeling reading time may require a balance between accurately predicting token probabilities and effectively incorporating time-related information. Given the limitations of current transformer-based models in this area, further research is needed to improve their ability to replicate human reading behavior. The code used in this study will be made available for public use.

Research has shown that botnets often utilize the same command structure, and these patterns can be leveraged to identify bot groups by analyzing honeypot command sequences. Our study employs natural language processing techniques to examine honeypot command records from a global honeypot network, applying techniques like tokenization, part-of-speech analysis, and n-gram analysis to detect patterns in botnet activity. Our findings indicate that machine learning models trained on honeypot command data can effectively identify botnet activity, and we also explore the feasibility of using honeypot data to detect emerging malware. Our research contributes to the development of a more effective method for identifying botnets, and we share our findings with the honeypot community. The Earth observation network, comprised of multiple satellite systems like Sentinel-2, is a valuable resource for tracking changes in land cover, land use, and crop health. However, the sheer volume of images generated daily poses a challenge to analysts, who must rapidly process large datasets to provide timely insights. To address this issue, we are developing EarthNets, an innovative platform that utilizes AI to streamline the image analysis process. By leveraging a semi-supervised machine learning approach, EarthNets can automatically identify areas of interest and extract relevant features, such as those indicative of deforestation. Our goal is to empower analysts with actionable information, enabling rapid decision-making. Initially, we are focusing on satellite-based monitoring of forest fires, agricultural health, and oceanic phenomena like sea-level rise, oceanic plastics, and algal blooms. Once developed, EarthNets will provide a unified interface for data visualization, analysis, and AI-driven decision support, allowing users to investigate, visualize, and explore the vast dataset. Ultimately, this project aims to make satellite image analysis more accessible, efficient, and sustainable. As such, this paper serves as a project proposal for the 2020 Earth Observation Science Challenge, Earth Observation for Critical Zone Science, and serves as an initial report on our ongoing research. Further details regarding the project will be presented in subsequent publications. We are seeking the support of the community to help us bring this ambitious project to life. Unlike conventional methods, our approach eliminates redundant filters by quantifying the degree of filter interrelation using a Self-Affinity Matrix (SAM). This matrix represents the interdependencies between filters based on their input and output correlations. Our method prioritizes the least influential filters, ensuring minimal disruption to the network's original performance. Experimental evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet datasets reveal that our approach achieves an average model compression of 34.6%, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available for public access at https://github.com/ChenChengHB/SAM-based_filter_thinning. Furthermore, our approach can be extended to other deep learning structures, such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). By applying our method to RNNs, we achieve an average model compression of 14.1% while maintaining similar performance levels as the original model. This research has been accepted for publication in the Journal of Systems Science & Control (JSSC) under the Elsevier B.V. publication platform. The key contributions of our work are as follows:

4.  A method for prioritizing the least influential filters has been proposed, yielding a model compression rate of 34.6%.

Deep neural networks often struggle with high computational and memory demands due to their extensive parameterization. Reducing these demands through feature compression can lead to significant performance degradation. In this research, we address this challenge by developing a method that compresses network parameters while maintaining accurate classification performance. Our approach involves merging multiple neural networks into a single, unified network with shared weights, achieved by synchronizing the hidden unit representations during training. This synchronization occurs naturally in the feature space without requiring additional regularization, as units with similar features are grouped together. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively reduces model size with minimal accuracy loss, surpassing alternative approaches in various computer vision tasks. Our proposed method is also applicable to natural language processing tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our code is available for public access.

A novel theory known as resilient limit evaluation theory (ReLEviT) has been developed to efficiently determine the worst-case loads in structures with variable properties. This theory is an extension of limit evaluation theory (LEviT) and considers the worst-case scenario under parameter uncertainties. ReLEviT achieves this by analyzing the worst-case behavior of limit load-bearing mechanisms, rather than the random field itself, to estimate the worst-case load value. The proposed attack has been successfully tested on various models, including those used for image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, and yielded impressive results in manipulating the desired output. Furthermore, experiments involving multiple attack objectives and multiple target models demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach. Ultimately, this innovative technique empowers attackers to manipulate a wide range of machine learning models, posing a significant threat to the security of deep learning systems. Given the ease with which this attack can be performed, even for those without extensive knowledge of machine learning, it is likely to be exploited in the future. A novel approach to estimating metabolic rates in Escherichia coli grown in limited culture, utilizing a minimum of information, is presented. The proposed method leverages a Maximum Entropy Principle to derive the system's response to nutrient scarcity, considering the energy expenditure as a variable that maximizes uncertainty. The technique is validated by comparing estimated metabolic rates with those determined through direct calculation from mass balances in experiments conducted with Escherichia coli grown in environments with restricted glucose and biotin availability. The results indicate that this method accurately estimates metabolic rates within an average margin of error, particularly in scenarios where direct calculations are feasible, thereby demonstrating its potential as a reliable alternative in scenarios where detailed mass balance data are limited. The technique is further enhanced by integrating a dynamic model of cellular metabolism to facilitate the estimation of metabolic fluxes in real-time, thereby enabling the development of predictive control strategies for biotechnological applications. The proposed method is also applicable to other microorganisms and may be extended to accommodate nutrient-restricted continuous cultures in diverse fields. Machine learning models have shown great success in handling complex data sets,
but they can be easily deceived by malicious users who manipulate the
information to influence model predictions, often for financial gain. This type
of data poisoning, particularly prevalent in tabular information, poses a
significant challenge for machine learning practitioners. In this paper, we
investigate a specific form of adversarial attacks, referred to as "antagonistic
assaults," which involve manipulating training data to maximize the error of a
target model. We demonstrate how antagonistic assaults can be applied to
diagnose and prevent fraudulent activities, and provide a comprehensive
analysis of the limitations and biases inherent in data sets with uneven
distribution. Furthermore, our study highlights the potential for antagonistic
assaults to serve as a defense mechanism against adversarial attacks and
offers a novel approach to identifying and addressing data imbalance issues. The
findings of this research have significant implications for the development of
robust machine learning systems capable of handling data manipulation and
handling imbalanced data sets. Ultimately, our study provides a fresh
perspective on the importance of data quality in machine learning research and
offers a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges associated with
handling tabular information. The code for this research is available on

Energy system models frequently utilize time series data to forecast energy demand and generate schedule predictions for energy production with varying operational times. To reduce computational costs, these models typically employ discrete time steps, necessitating the representation of continuous time series as discrete points within a lower-dimensional space. In this study, we propose an approach that integrates autoencoders and cluster analysis to select representative intervals for energy system modeling. By leveraging autoencoders to compress high-dimensional data and cluster analysis to identify similar patterns, our method efficiently selects a limited number of discrete points to represent numerous time series at various intervals. Through a case study involving wind power prediction, our approach demonstrated its ability to reduce computational costs while maintaining accurate predictions. Furthermore, our method was applied to energy system planning to select optimal intervals for planning, resulting in significant improvements in computational efficiency. By scaling up the analysis to larger geographical areas, our approach can be utilized to optimize energy system planning at larger spatial scales. Overall, our method provides a practical solution for dimensionally reducing high-dimensional data while preserving the inherent structure of the data. In the context of sparse array codes, vectorization significantly accelerates processing by reducing the need for iterative loops. Achieving high performance on vector processors requires a detailed analysis of data dependencies within kernel functions. This paper presents a record analysis method that identifies and captures these dependencies, allowing for the ideal distribution of data transformations across the processor. By leveraging this approach, vector processors can efficiently execute vectorized code and deliver optimal performance. Our results demonstrate substantial performance gains, with speedups of up to 3.2x and 2.8x on vector processors compared to the Intel Xeon processor. Moreover, our approach enables efficient processing of large datasets that exceed processor and memory limitations, with a near-linear speedup of 7x on a dataset 64 times larger than a standard reference dataset. This work also applies to other sparse array codes, such as the SCDM code, resulting in a 2.5x speedup on a vector processor. Our record analysis framework is a versatile and reusable tool that can enhance the performance of various sparse array codes. In a scenario where multiple vehicles connected to each other through a reliable wireless link participate in federated training with limited backhaul connectivity, we examine an approach to leveraging this network structure for edge computing. By utilizing the vehicles' local computation capabilities and exchange of model updates via direct links, we investigate under what conditions this setup allows for edge computing. Our focus is on a scenario where vehicles have limited computation resources and power, making centralized optimization impractical. Instead, we propose a decentralized method that involves each vehicle running a local version of the federated optimization algorithm. Our results, derived through analysis and simulation, indicate that this approach can achieve comparable performance to more centralized methods in most cases, even under highly mobile conditions. The key to this performance is the vehicles' use of large batch sizes, combined with strategic selection of forward and backward training tasks. Our study also reveals that, while linked vehicles can perform well with limited backhaul connectivity, unconnected vehicles face significant challenges in achieving acceptable performance under similar conditions. Our findings suggest that highly mobile, unconnected vehicles may require alternative approaches to edge computing. One such alternative is a 'train-merge-train' strategy, where vehicles temporarily group to enhance backhaul capabilities, although this approach comes with increased energy costs due to the additional communication overhead. The results of our research are intended to provide insights for future studies on the design of mobile networks for edge computing. a detailed breakdown of the various contributions to the QCD pressure, which

the electromagnetic force. Our analysis also includes a comparison with theoretical
predictions and a discussion of the implications of our findings for the study
of QCD thermodynamics and heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, we have made our

Our results also suggest that the protocol's performance characteristics are unaffected by different edge servers' configurations.  Overall, our evaluation confirms that the proposed protocol is a viable and efficient solution for providing secure LBS. The discovery ratio, a novel measure of test power, has gained significant attention in the scientific community for evaluating the effectiveness of significance tests. However, a recent study revealed that the discovery ratio exhibits inherent uncertainties when sample sizes are finite, leading to inaccurate power assessments. Building upon this work, our investigation expands on the discovery ratio's uncertainties in the context of dependent $t$-tests, where paired or repeated samples are involved. Our findings indicate that the discovery ratio can yield misleading power estimates, with the degree of uncertainty influenced by the correlation between paired samples and the ratio of the non-centrality parameter to the centrality parameter. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the discovery ratio's associated variance can be approximated using a specific formula. Notably, our results suggest that the discovery ratio may underestimate power in certain scenarios, but overestimate it in others. Ultimately, our study provides valuable insights into the discovery ratio's limitations and uncertainties in the context of dependent $t$-tests, contributing to a deeper understanding of its potential applications and misapplications in practice. We utilize operator representation to analyze spinor fields that have a higher order of spinor complexity. In our previous work, we established a representation for the Dirac operator within the framework of non-standard quaternionic operator functions. Building on this foundation, we now apply similar techniques to the higher order Rarita-Schwinger operator, as well as the Fierz-Pauli operator, in the context of non-commutative spaces. Following this, we examine the representation of these operators on the Manin module, a structure that generalizes the concept of modules in non-commutative geometry. Notably, we find that the Manin module representation of operators aligns with conventional operator representation, except for the presence of additional terms. We also discuss the representation of energy-momentum and angular momentum operators, including their commutators, and provide a concrete example by considering a specific combination of these operators. Finally, we outline potential avenues for extending our representation scheme to other complex spinor fields. 

Keywords: non-standard quaternionic operator functions, operator representation, non-commutative spaces, Manin module, spinor complexity.

A novel approach for estimating the free energy of medication solvation in supercritical CO2 is proposed, utilizing molecular dynamics simulations, but this time, the method is designed to be less computationally expensive by comparing potential interaction energies between solutes in CO2 and a reference solvent, typically water. This method is validated through comparison with all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, but it also shows promise for use with alternative molecular models, such as coarse-grain models, which provide a significant reduction in computational requirements, as demonstrated in this research. Coarse-grain models, like the Gay-Berne model, were found to accurately predict solvation free energies, as they produced values within 1 kcal/mol of all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, as long as the solvent molecules' mobility is not overly restricted. which leverages a deep neural network to clean images by exploiting the 
sensitivity of image content to spatial disturbances. This method operates without 
using any reference clean images and is based on the idea that noise levels 
increase with the magnitude of spatial disturbances. As a result, a noisy image 
can be represented as a linear combination of clean images and noise terms, 
with the coefficients of this combination decreasing as noise levels increase.

linear combination, and we use a regularization technique to ensure that the 
coefficients are well-estimated. Notably, this approach is effective in scenarios where

integrated with existing image denoising techniques. Experimental results on widely

denoising methods in terms of image quality. Additionally, our approach is computationally

Generative design platforms empower designers to create innovative concepts by defining parameters and rules for design processes. To streamline this process, researchers have developed self-learning algorithms that can autonomously generate design options based on user-provided prompts. However, these systems require extensive training data and expertise from both design professionals and machine learning specialists. To address this challenge, this study proposes a new approach that enables non-experts to create and annotate large datasets for generative design, leveraging the capabilities of language models to generate potential designs and guide the annotation process. This method is demonstrated through a case study on residential building design, where novice users successfully generated and annotated design data, resulting in a functional generative design model. This research aims to make generative design more accessible by reducing the technical barriers associated with data collection and algorithm development. Furthermore, it explores the potential applications of this approach in other domains, such as medical imaging and product design. In this research, we introduce an innovative approach to training autonomous driving systems that can learn to follow diverse traffic rules across multiple countries by leveraging the expertise of local drivers. The key concept is to empower humans, represented as expert drivers, and enable them to influence the development of policies in line with local regulations. To achieve this, we propose a framework that utilizes Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, where drivers collaborate to create a global policy that conforms to specific rules while adapting to changing traffic conditions. To address the complexity of this multi-agent setup, we employ a hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning approach, resulting in a scalable solution. Our framework's effectiveness is evaluated using a large-scale dataset of German and Indian traffic rules, demonstrating its ability to learn and apply the correct rules in various scenarios. Our results show that this approach leads to more efficient learning, increased human involvement, and improved adaptability to new situations. Galaxy groups serve as an alternative to galaxy clusters for studying the universe's expansion, but they are subject to various uncertainties. These uncertainties stem from two sources: first, theoretical limitations in describing group evolution, and second, empirical challenges arising from discrepancies in galaxy distributions within groups. To enhance semi-supervised learning, we introduce an approach called FlexMatch. This method involves a two-part framework where the first phase utilizes a curriculum learning strategy to progressively increase the difficulty of the training samples for accurate predictions. In the second phase, the model is further fine-tuned using a combination of pseudo labels generated from a teacher model and a loss function that rewards confident predictions. To optimize performance, the samples used in the curriculum learning approach are ranked by their difficulty, with an emphasis on using easier, less ambiguous examples to improve model accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate FlexMatch's effectiveness in improving model accuracy and robustness across various tasks, including image recognition and text classification. Notably, the method achieves state-of-the-art results on the ImageNet-1K classification task, with FlexMatch outperforming a baseline model by 1.7% in absolute top-1 accuracy. Additionally, the approach has been successfully applied to the domain of self-supervised learning, resulting in a 4.8% improvement in absolute average mean squared error when compared to a baseline model. This research introduces a novel, dynamic network architecture for forecasting
traffic disruptions at an early stage. The proposed model, Dynamic Spatio-Temporal
Focus Network (DSToFN), is designed to learn traffic patterns and anticipate
future conditions. By integrating spatial-temporal features and focusing on key
areas, DSToFN enhances its capacity to predict traffic conditions and identify
incidents more accurately. The architecture consists of two key components:
RNNFocus and CNNFocus networks, which capture spatial-temporal information, and
a fusion module that combines their results. The DSToFN model outperforms
existing methods in predicting traffic conditions and identifying incidents early.

Author metrics for assessing an author's performance have gained widespread
acceptance within academia, despite their limitations and potential for abuse.
Building upon these metrics, new criteria are emerging to evaluate an author's
contribution to science, such as citation metrics and peer review ratings.
This research aims to introduce a clear framework for evaluating an author's
impact by analyzing and predicting their future research output. We examine
the effectiveness of various metrics, including those based on citation numbers
and their growth, in accurately predicting an author's future research.
Notably, our results indicate that a simple metric - the h-index - offers the
best prediction of future research output among the tested methods. Additionally,
our analysis explores the potential benefits and drawbacks of incorporating
novel metrics, such as those based on author influence and research maturity,
into the author evaluation process. We also discuss the potential applications
of this research in promoting fairness and accountability within the peer review
process. Ultimately, our findings suggest that a more nuanced approach to
author evaluation is necessary, one that takes into account the complexity of
scientific impact and the need for a more systematic assessment of an author's
contribution to science. This research offers a foundation for revisiting the
role of author evaluation in academia. The associated codebase is available at

our results at https://github.com/zhuyiwan/prediction_of_future_performance. The

We propose a method for refining policies in Markov Decision Processes, which we call enhancement. This approach involves a master algorithm that uses a policy gradient method to optimize the expected value of a reward function, which is computed by a learner algorithm that determines the expected value of a function, which in turn is derived from the state distribution. Our approach is notable for its theoretical guarantees, including its ability to prove the convergence acceleration and its independence from the size of the state space. This is achieved by analyzing the behavior of the two algorithms over time, which we categorize into a "hot" phase where the master algorithm dominates and a "cold" phase where the learner algorithm does so. Our approach is also extended to handle Markov Decision Processes with restrictions, which are those that do not allow a policy to transition the system out of a restricted subset. This is done by modifying the reward function to penalize such transitions. Our results show that our approach can accelerate policy convergence and our findings are supported by numerical experiments. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of our approach to a real-world problem, namely the portfolio optimization problem. The growing adoption of intelligent meter networks (IMNs) for smart grid applications necessitates a more efficient data transmission approach to mitigate the high communication burden. As the primary function of IMNs is to collect and transmit metering data from various nodes, data reduction techniques are essential to minimize the load on the network. Anomaly detection in these networks often generates a higher volume of data, including both normal and anomalous data, due to the identification of potential security threats. This increased data transmission burden further exacerbates the already high load, posing a challenge for IMNs. To address this issue, this study proposes an adaptive data transmission mechanism for intelligent meter networks, designed to optimize data reduction and transmission efficiency in response to anomaly detection. This proposed approach is evaluated through simulations using a software-defined network simulator, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in minimizing data overload and enhancing the overall performance of the IMN. The experimental findings indicate that the proposed adaptive data transmission mechanism outperforms traditional data transmission methods in various scenarios, including both anomaly-detection and no-anomaly-detection cases. Moreover, the results show that the proposed approach yields better results in terms of transmission delay, data volume, and energy consumption compared to the conventional methods. The promising outcomes of this study suggest its potential to improve the performance of IMNs in smart grid environments. The code and simulation results used in this study are available on GitHub. This paper presents a novel active learning approach grounded in the concept that the quality of feedback is paramount in determining a learner's effectiveness. The primary objective is to develop an active learning method that maximizes the learning potential of a student, given a fixed budget for feedback. To achieve this, we have devised an active learning strategy that prioritizes instances where the feedback is most likely to be highly effective, thereby enhancing the learner's overall performance. The proposed method is evaluated using various datasets and a real-world student assessment dataset, and the results indicate that our approach surpasses traditional active learning techniques in improving both query performance and learner performance. Additionally, we have discovered that leveraging feedback quality as a guiding principle for active learning yields superior outcomes compared to relying solely on diversity. The underlying assumption is that the feedback quality is directly correlated with the learner's performance. Notably, we have observed that our approach is particularly effective in scenarios where the feedback is limited, and we provide insights into how this method can be adapted for educational settings, where the budget for feedback is inherently constrained. Future research directions are also discussed. The key contributions of this paper are threefold: firstly, we have developed a novel active learning strategy that prioritizes instances with high feedback quality; secondly, we have demonstrated that our approach is particularly effective in the context of educational settings; and thirdly, we have established a connection between our method and the learner's performance. The findings of this study are of particular interest to researchers in the active learning domain, as well as educators seeking to optimize the learning process. This paper outlines a range of relational tasks within the framework of Functional Ontological Mathematics (FOLE). Furthermore, we discuss the potential for these relational tasks to inform the design of real-valued learning models. This research marks a significant advancement towards a comprehensive learning theory framework applicable to the analysis of real numbers. We explore the connection between the topological properties of a quantum many-body state and the trapping of atoms and molecules within three-dimensional spatial arrangements. Specifically, we analyze the behavior of quantum matter in environments resembling knots, links, and labyrinthine pathways, examining how these structures influence the entrapment of bosons and fermions. The resulting analysis offers a novel quantitative assessment of a quantum state's topological complexity, grounded in empirical evidence rather than traditional entanglement metrics. Our research demonstrates that certain types of tangles significantly impact entrapment, and we propose a related measure that may provide valuable insights into the complex interactions within many-body systems. The findings are relevant to recent advancements in generating and studying topological states in cold atom systems. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications of our research in the development of topological quantum sensors. The methods employed in this study are adaptable to diverse physical systems, including those in condensed matter, high-energy physics, and quantum foundations, as well as to the manipulation of complex systems in biology and materials science. Ultimately, we discuss the broader implications of our research, including its potential contributions to the development of topological quantum technologies. This research examines statistical compressed sensing of complex Gaussian blend models, which involve a mixture of $K$ Gaussian distributions with unique means and covariance structures. By assuming that the blend model can be represented by a limited number of $s$ nonzero features with respect to a general dictionary $A$, we propose a maximum a posteriori estimation method that utilizes a hierarchical model to estimate the blend model parameters. The approach involves a two-stage optimization process that alternates between estimating the mean and covariance of the distributions, as well as the weights and coefficients of the non-zero features. We derive a non-asymptotic minimax risk bound for the recovery error rate, which scales with $\log(1/\delta)$ as the sample size grows. The results demonstrate that the method can accurately estimate the non-zero features with high probability, subject to certain conditions on the number of samples and the signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings and assess the method's performance in recovering the non-zero features. The approach is also extended to estimate the dictionary $A$ when its structure is unknown. Additionally, the method is applied to a real-world application, specifically image segmentation, where it is used to reconstruct high-dimensional images from compressed measurements. The results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in reconstructing the images and estimating the non-zero features. Finally, the method is shown to be robust to various noise models and robust to a range of values for $s$. Overall, the method provides a new approach to statistical compressed sensing of complex Gaussian models, which can accurately recover the non-zero features and estimate the model parameters. The approach has the potential to be applied to a range of applications, including image segmentation, data denoising, and classification. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved the accuracy of forecasting future locations for moving objects. However, most existing methods focus on predicting a single future trajectory, neglecting the inherent uncertainty inherent in forecasting processes. In many applications, forecasting multiple trajectories is crucial, as it allows for a better understanding of uncertainty. In this paper, we address the task of multi-outcome trajectory forecasting, referred to as M-TRF, and propose a novel framework called GED-TRF. The GED-TRF framework is an encoder-decoder architecture that incorporates a graph neural network to learn the latent relationships between features and predicts future trajectories for multiple targets. Experimental results on large datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach. Furthermore, we also explore the impact of forecasting multiple outcomes on real-world applications, such as traffic prediction and ride-hailing demand. The source code for GED-TRF is publicly available. This research marks the first study on multi-outcome trajectory forecasting, and we anticipate that our work will inspire further research in this area. This paper introduces a novel nonparametric approach for estimating the multivariate mixing distribution in continuous-time mixing processes. A particle filter-based method is developed to approximate the univariate conditional distribution of the mixing variable given observed data, which is crucial for determining the mixing distribution. Utilizing this approximation, we propose a series of multivariate goodness-of-fit test statistics to evaluate the alignment of the data with a wide range of multivariate mixing distributions. Our proposed method is supported by an asymptotic theoretical framework, comprehensive simulation studies, and an application to real-world data analysis. Furthermore, we extend this approach to the sequential assessment of mixing distributions in real-time applications. This research is exemplified through its application to the analysis of daily rainfall data. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in identifying the most suitable mixing distribution for the data at hand. Moreover, we successfully applied our nonparametric approach to the real-time prediction of daily rainfall patterns in a specific region. Our results show that the multivariate mixing distribution of the daily rainfall patterns varies significantly across different locations within the region. Consequently, we were able to provide accurate location-specific predictions of the daily rainfall patterns under different mixing distributions. Overall, the proposed method offers a versatile and efficient approach for nonparametric assessment of multivariate mixing distributions, which is particularly useful in real-time data analysis and prediction applications. Finally, we highlight the adaptability of the proposed method, which can be easily adapted to other types of multivariate time series data. However, we also note that the proposed method is computationally intensive and may be limited by the number of particles used. Therefore, we recommend the use of a large number of particles to achieve accurate approximations of the univariate conditional distributions. Additionally, we recommend the use of a time-varying approach to the multivariate mixing distribution to capture the dynamic nature of the data. This is particularly relevant in real-time data analysis and prediction applications where the mixing distribution may change over time. Recent advancements in neural networks have led to significant performance improvements in video compression, but their practical application is hindered by their large size and vulnerability to changes in hyperparameters. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a new approach called Gemino, which leverages the efficiency of low-bitwidth quantization and model distillation to compress neural networks. By quantizing multiple key components, Gemino achieves a substantial reduction in model size, from 5.5MB to 0.5MB, with minimal impact on video quality. Furthermore, Gemino employs distillation to transfer knowledge from large neural networks, resulting in a single model that combines high compression efficiency and performance. Our evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of Gemino, which outperforms state-of-the-art video compression methods, such as BVI, H.266-VT, and MPEG-I, in terms of PSNR and SSIM metrics. Notably, Gemino exhibits exceptional robustness under various hyperparameter settings and different bitrates, making it a promising solution for future video compression applications. The integration of machine learning algorithms in the geoscience field has been rapidly adopted, particularly in the analysis of seismic data, due to their ability to simplify complex tasks. However, implementing these algorithms in a way that allows geoscine researchers to understand their inner workings is crucial. This research proposes a novel approach that combines a Collaborative Inversion-Segmentation method with a human-centered collaborative framework. This method enables geoscience experts to leverage machine learning tools, such as neural networks, without losing their interpretability. By applying a neural network to invert seismic data, a segmentation map is generated that highlights the structure of the subsurface. This segmentation map is then used to create a geological interpretation, which is further refined by the human expert. This refinement process is then fed back into the neural network, allowing it to generate a more accurate interpretation. This process can be repeated, creating a feedback loop between the neural network and human expert. This collaborative approach has been tested on a real-world dataset and has shown promising results. The paper concludes by discussing potential future applications of this method. We introduce ViT-BEVSeg, a transformer-based framework for aerial monocular segmentation. This model leverages the transformer's ability to generate contextual representations and pairs it with a spatial attention mechanism to efficiently handle large input sequences. To further enhance performance, ViT-BEVSeg incorporates a hierarchical multi-scale feature extraction approach, which includes a multi-scale feature fusion module and a multi-resolution feature fusion module. These components enable the network to capture both local and global context. Experimental evaluations on the Semantic Segmentation in Building Environments dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of ViT-BEVSeg, yielding a top accuracy of 85.8%, which surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the network's efficiency is validated through ablation studies. Notably, ViT-BEVSeg achieves superior performance while being significantly more efficient than its competitors, primarily due to its reduced number of parameters and lower computational requirements. The objective of open-set identification is to determine if incoming data points belong to a known class set. Unlike anomaly detection, distinguishing normal from abnormal data requires a labelable abnormal dataset. This distinction makes open-set identification a more challenging task. Current methods often rely on complex, feature-dependent models that struggle to adapt to changes in data distribution. In contrast, our proposed approach, ASI, uses a straightforward, feature-invariant model to learn similarity and identify out-of-domain data. ASI achieves this by leveraging a similarity metric and a neural network augmentation module that generates similar examples from a limited set of training images. This approach enables efficient learning of similarity and effective identification of open-set boundaries. Experimental results demonstrate ASI's state-of-the-art performance on various benchmark datasets. Furthermore, our proposed method's ability to learn similarity across different classes and datasets has shown to be generalizable and effective in a wide range of applications.
